name: Registro Nacional compliance keeper for private-security companies (alta/baja, uniforms, vehicles, branches, training)
buyer: Authorised private-security firms (federal authorisation for 2+ states, or state-licensed single-state firms), usually small, family-owned guard companies
trigger: Ley Federal de Seguridad Privada art. 10 and Reglamento arts. 32-34 (electronic or printed records of alta/baja with cause, uniform models, vehicles, arms, radios, training and medical/psych/toxicology evaluations). DGSP publishes sanctions in the DOF in 2026, for example omitting the baja of 112 uniforms and of two branches, and a fine of 1,000 UMA in Feb 2026. Ley General del SNSP also requires sharing personnel and equipment data with the Secretariado Ejecutivo. The Ley General de Seguridad Privada was not yet in force when last found.
evidence: https://mley.mx/Reg_LFSP/articulo/32/ ; https://mley.mx/Reg_LFSP/articulo/33/ ; https://mley.mx/Reg_LFSP/articulo/34/ ; https://mley.mx/LFSP/articulo/10/ ; https://www.ejecentral.com.mx/regularan-servicios-de-seguridad-privada-en-mexico ; https://sidof.segob.gob.mx/notas/docFuente/5798715 (2026 sanctions, snippet only)
existing: Competitor search in Spanish ('software seguridad privada control de personal uniformes altas bajas Registro Nacional DGSP') returned only generic uniform-management software and the regulation texts. No Mexican product specific to the Registro Nacional found, but guard-company payroll and scheduling tools were not checked.
unchecked: Number of authorised firms (federal list and state lists), whether DGSP has an electronic submission portal or only paper/CD formats, state-level duties in each of the 32 states, status of the Ley General de Seguridad Privada, and guard-management or payroll tools that already export to DGSP.

first_check.duty: LFSP art. 32 (prestador obligations) and Reglamento arts. 32-34: register altas/bajas with the cause, plus uniforms, vehicles, arms and radios, in the Registro Nacional de Empresas, Personal y Equipo de Seguridad Privada, on electronic or printed forms. Operational staff need annual medical, psychological and toxicology exams. Written notices are due within 3 business days for theft or loss of documents or IDs and for suspension of activities, and within 5 for asset-disposal orders. Firms must tell the state authority about a federal authorisation within 30 days. Modality VI firms file a buyer registry every 6 months. Altas/bajas have no fixed deadline, so they are event-driven. Penalties under LFSP art. 42 run from amonestación to fines and suspension or revocation. Enforcement is current: DGSP file DGSP/DELC/PAS/169/2026 (28 Aug 2026) gave GCH Seguridad Privada an amonestación for not reporting the baja of 112 uniforms. I could not verify the claim's 1,000 UMA fine. I found no source showing that a Ley General de Seguridad Privada has been published. A Senate bill passed in 2018, but nothing confirms it was enacted, so the LFSP still applies.
first_check.market: I found no official 2025/2026 count. A commercial training site claims about 8,500 authorised firms employing more than 600,000 guards, citing the Registro Nacional; this is unofficial. Jalisco: 289 firms, 83 of them state-authorised (nmas.com.mx, date unclear). The DGSP open-data list of federally authorised firms was last updated in Oct 2018 and gives no total on the page. Each of the 32 states also licenses single-state firms under its own law, for example Nuevo León and Estado de México.
first_check.competitor: I found no Mexican product that prepares or keeps DGSP Registro Nacional filings. Generic guard-operations software (GuardsPro/Guardso, CGuardPro, OfficerReports) covers patrols, shifts and incident reports and does not mention the DGSP or the Registro. Not reached: whether the DGSP/SSPC runs an online filing portal (the Reglamento allows electronic or printed forms), and Mexican payroll/HR vendors for guard companies that may export DGSP formats. Both are risks to check.
first_check.reason: The duty is real and in force under the Ley Federal de Seguridad Privada (last reformed in 2011) and its Reglamento. Firms must record personnel altas/bajas with the cause, uniforms, vehicles, arms and radios in the Registro Nacional, and give operational staff annual medical, psychological and toxicology exams. The DGSP enforces it: in Aug 2026 GCH Seguridad Privada received a public amonestación for not reporting the baja of 112 uniforms. Weaknesses: the rules set no fixed deadline for altas/bajas, so the work is event-driven, and the sanction I verified was a warning, not a fine. I found no DGSP-specific Mexican software. Generic guard tools (GuardsPro, CGuardPro) don't cover the Registro. I couldn't confirm whether the DGSP has an online filing portal. The market of about 8,500 firms is an unofficial figure.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Not settled: whether SSPC/DGSP runs an online filing portal (no evidence either way), and whether state portals such as CDMX's or Baja California's monthly report already digitise filing. I could not read the Baja California guide because the PDF fetch returned binary data.
challenge_check.reason: I found nothing that kills the idea. The Ley Federal de Seguridad Privada still applies: its last reform was in 2011, and DOF sanctions in 2026 cite it. I found no sign that the Ley General de Seguridad Privada was enacted. DGSP enforces the alta/baja duty. One 2026 DOF sanction punished a firm that didn't keep its personnel and arms status up to date, and search snippets mention unreported bajas of 114 staff and 112 uniforms. I found no SSPC or DGSP online filing portal and no Mexican vendor that targets DGSP filings. Generic guard software (C-Guard Pro, GuardsPro) does patrols, shifts and payroll. Risks: there is no reliable firm count (the 8,500 figure comes from an unsourced blog; Jalisco has 289 firms and Chihuahua 269), filing rules differ by state, local gestores may already do this work, and willingness to pay is unclear.
